lawyer: Dr. Rafiqur Rahman with Dr. Mohammad Shamsul Aim Advocates — For the Petitioner
parties:
Baitul Aman Co-operative Housing Society Ltd.  ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Additional District Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka and others  ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Anwarul Haque Chowdhury J : This is an application under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and is directed against a judgment and order dated 14.7.93 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka in Miscellaneous Non-Judicial Case No. 1 of 1990. 

 3. Respondent No. 2 Mrs. Shahanara Begum, wife of late Abdul Gafur of E-1/D, T&T Colony, Maghbazer, Dhaka, filed a dispute case under section 86 of the Co-operative Societies Act before the District Co-operative Officer alleging that she being a member of the society had obtained allotment of plot No. 19. She paid all the charges and paid Taka 600.00 out of Taka 1800.00 against development charge and that after being registered, the symbolic possession of the plot was given to her. Subsequently, she had paid the rest amount of Taka 1200.00 in the month of February 1974 but actual possession was not handed over to her till that date. It is the allegation of the said Mrs. Shahanara Begum that the authority of the society changed the number of plots and upon application filed by her before the Registrar Co-operative Societies in 1979, the Assistant Registrar Co-operative Societies made enquiry and directed the authority concerned to hand over possession of the said plot in her favour. But the authority did not comply with the same. Subsequently upon another application filed by her the District Co-operative Societies after holding enquiry directed the authority concerned to.hand over possession of the said plot. 

 4. The District Co-operative Officer, Dhaka on receipt of the said dispute case referred the same to the Deputy Assistant Registrar Co-operative Societies appointing him as Arbitrator. Before the Arbitrator the petitioner society appeared but the Arbitrator without hearing communicated back by saying that it was very difficult to settle the dispute case within the frame-work of the Co-operative Law and Rules as it involves revenue and settlement laws 

 5. On 9.4.90 the District Co-operative Officer, Dhaka referred the said dispute case to the District Judge, Dhaka for disposal under section 89(a) of the Co-operative Societies Ordinance. The learned District Judge on receipt of the same record registered the said dispute case as Miscellaneous Non-Judicial Case No. 1 of 1990 and transferred the same to the court of the learned Additional District Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka for disposal. 

 6. The petitioner society appeared before the learned Additional District Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka and contested the said Misc. case by filling written objection denying the material allegations made in the petition. It was their case that the case is not maintainable in the present form and nature and she the petitioner had no locus standi to file the instant case and the petitioner Shahanara Begum is not entitled to have any relief on false, fictitious, fanciful and motivated statements made in the petition, and that plot No. 19 was allotted to her and an agreement was executed and registered and it was stipulated in paragraph 1 that the petitioner should pay Taka 1200.00 but despite repeated calls the petitioner Mrs. Shahanara Begum failed to pay the money which prompted the authority of the society to serve a notice on 9.11.70 upon her to the effect that measures that might go against their interest, would be taken against the member who would fail to pay the development charge by 15.12.70. It was thereafter extended upto 21.1.71 and since the petitioner failed to pay the development charge within the stipulated time and even failed to pay the monthly subscription, she lost her right to have any plot. 

 7. The learned Additional District Judge heard the miscellaneous case and after hearing the parties allowed the Miscellaneous case by judgment and order dated 14.6.93 directing the petitioner society to hand over possession of plot No. 19 (new 333) in favour of Mrs. Shahanara Begum within one month from date of the order, against which judgment and order of the court, this petition is moved in court today under Article 102 of the Constitution and obviously not in mandamus but in certiorari. 

 8. He have heard the learned Counsel Dr. Rafiqur Rahman, gone through the averments made in the petition and the annexures and considered the submissions of the learned Counsel who submitted that in the instant case the court had no jurisdiction to entertain the matter because a proceeding had been initiated by the Additional Deputy Registrar who is not the legally competent authority under the Co-operative Society Act and Ordinance to initiate such and there having existed jurisdictional error, this petition under certiorari would be maintainable. Dr. Rafiqur Rahman further submitted that when a court has no jurisdiction the jurisdiction would not be conferred upon the court by the consent of the party. As to the merits he submitted that the judgment of the court below is without any evidence and the court had not appreciated the -plea of the society as in their written statement before the court which is to the effect that the petitioner Mrs. Shahanara Begum having not paid the required amount she has lost her right long ago. It is the further submission of the learned Advocate that the learned Judge committed illegality in directing the petitioner society to hand over possession of plot No. 19, now plot No. 333 without being satisfied as to the existence of any such plot by holding any local investigation. The petitioner before the learned Court of Additional District Judge had a duty to prove his case and it cannot be proved by mere conjectures as was done in the instant case disposing of the case summarily. It is an illegality and is without lawful authority and thus of no legal effect. 

 12. This expression of lawful authority came to be examined before the Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case of Badrul Haque Khan vs. The Election Tribunal, reported in PLD 1963 (SC) 704. The Supreme Court proceeded to find out that an act of a judicial or of quasi-judicial body can be held without lawful authority only after bearing in mind the nature of the authority vested in such body. Admission of inadmissible evidence is not an act without lawful authority and in every case the erroneous decision on a point of law is not necessarily an act without lawful authority. Kaikaus, J. in the said judgment has referred to the Privy Council case of Natbell Liquors Ltd. It was urged in that case that this was a clear error of law and such an error would make the decision without lawful authority. The Supreme Court held that this proposition is indisputable that when there is jurisdiction to decide a particular matter then there is jurisdiction to decide it rightly or wrongly and the fact that the decision is incorrect does not render the decision without jurisdiction 

 13. Kaikaus, J. observed "I do not see any difference in a case where the question of law decided is a matter on which two opinions can easily be held and a case where the decision on a question of law appears to be clearly erroneous, unless a case of malafide or a more colourable exercise of jurisdiction could be made out, the decision would not be without lawful authority. If an order can be without legal authority because of a clearly wrong determination of a question of fact, there is no reason for any distinction in this connection between a decision on a question of law and a decision on question of fact. So if we were to accept the proposition that clearly erroneous decisions are without lawful authority, the court acting under Article 98 would constitute itself as a court of appeal for matters of fact as well as matters of law." 

 This case was again quoted with approval by another Bench of the Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case of Md. Hossain Munir vs. Sekandar, reported in PLD 1974 (SC) 139 and the court again examined the expression such as "without lawful authority and thus of no legal effect" as occurs in Article 102 (2)(a)(ii) of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh which was the same as under Article 98 of the Pakistan Constitution. After examining this expression their Lordships again held that the said expression is an expression of art and refers to jurisdiction so distinguished from mere erroneous decision on question of fact or even of law. The High Court in exercise of its jurisdiction under Article 98 is concerned only with the question whether a court or Tribunal below acted without its jurisdiction and a Tribunal having jurisdiction to decide the matter is competent to decide it rightly or wrongly and the mere fact that the decision is incorrect does not render the decision without lawful authority. 

 14. This court also in the case of Mustakim Ali vs. Abdul Motalib, in which one of us had been a party, had quoted with approval this decision of the Privy Council and decisions of the Supreme Court of Pakistan in holding that some erroneous decision would not be a matter for interference under certiorari though it can be examined on appeal. 

 15. In the instant case we, in our anxiety, had examined the Rules and Regulations under the Co-operative Society Act in order to find out whether the instant court had acted initially without jurisdiction, as it has been forcibly argued by the learned Counsel, and we find that under the provision of the Co-operative Society Ordinance, 1984 a dispute is to be referred to the Registrar touching the business or affairs of a Co-operative Society or of the Liquidator of a society. Under section 89 the mode of disposing of proceeding's under section 86 is that if any proceedings under section 80 the question at issue between the parties is one involving complicated question of law or of facts the Registrar may if he thinks fit either (a) stay the proceedings and refer the case to the District Judge for decisions whereupon the decision of the District Judge shall be final, (b) call upon one of the parties to institute a regular suit in civil Court for decision of the case within a period not exceeding six months to be fixed by himself and stay the proceedings, in the meanwhile, if no such suit is instituted within the period so fixed, the Registrar shall pass such order as he deems fit. The word Registrar has been defined to mean a person appointed to perform the duties of a Registrar of Co-operative Societies under the Ordinance and includes any person appointed to assist the Registrar upon whom all or any of the powers or duties of the Registrar referred to in section 7 have been or has been conferred or imposed under clause A of that section. In the instant case, it appears that this question of jurisdiction has not been taken for the first time. While examining this matter without really examining records which are not before us but only one-sided averment in the petition, we find that the respondent Mrs. Shahanara Begum filed an application before the Registrar, Co-operative Societies who made enquiry and directed the authority concerned to hand over the said plot in her favour which the authority did not comply. This has been clearly stated by the Co-operative Societies in para 4 under solemn affirmation and it is their case that the application was filed before the Registrar, Co-operative Societies in 1970 who is the proper forum to initiate, under section 86; a dispute is to be referred to the Registrar and the said has been done in the instant case and only because the Assistant Registrar made the enquiry the law shall not be violated because the Registrar did not always himself make any enquiry. He is supposed to work in co-operation with others who are subordinate to him. It appears further that upon non-compliance of the order of the office of the Registrar to hand over possession to Mrs. Shahanara Begum, she made another application and the Registrar, Co-operative Societies Dhaka held an enquiry and this has again been clearly stated in para 4 and thus it cannot be argued that the matter did not go before the proper forum namely, the Registrar and there is thus no violation of any procedure. The Co-operative Societies Authority and the Assistant Registrar are responsible Government Officers. They worked in this field for quite some time and they are perhaps, best to know the law and Rules and Regulations and they are presumed to have acted within jurisdiction and the law. It appears that the direction and order of the Co-operative Registrar had not been implemented by the present petitioner Society. It is provided in law that when a complicated question of law arises and cannot be settled only by an arbitrator, the proceeding be referred by the Registrar to the District Judge for decision and the District Judges decision shall be final. It appears from the petition that this dispute was referred by the District Co-operative Officer, Dhaka to the District Judge for disposal under section 89 and the District Judge, in turn, has referred the matter to the learned Court of Additional District Judge who heard the matter and delivered the judgment which is impugned before this Court, on the ground that Additional District Judge has exercised his power without jurisdiction because it has not been sent to him by proper authority and the matter has not been initiated in accordance with Rules and that the Court decided the matter without being satisfied as to the title of the petitioner in Miscellaneous case namely, Mrs. Shahanara Begum. 

 17. We do not find on merits that the court decided without evidence or misconstrued or misappropriated evidence or committed any error or law which however need not be gone into under certiorari. There is also nothing in the judgment which is "without lawful authority", as decided by the Supreme Court, referred to earlier.
